newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty holds breath as Czech crown again uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Zloty holds breath as Czech crown again uncertain.

text.p: The Polish zloty may again become vulnerable to a region-wide withdrawal if the Czech crown drops sharply as a result of a key confidence vote on Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's government next week, analysts said on Friday.

But zloty reaction to any fall in the crown would be less volatile than it was at the end of May because the bulk of more speculative foreigners had already sold their zloty-debt portfolios and Poland's fundamentals remained strong. @

"There is some talk of a further weakening of the crown, which could have a negative influence on the zloty, but the zloty should stay between 1.0 to 1.5 percent above parity," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA.
On Friday the zloty traded around the central bank-enforced resistance level of 1.5 percent above parity, underpinned by foreign purchases of Polish fixed bonds earlier this week.

"At times, zloty appreciation pressure briefly appeared and pushed the market into intervention territory, but trading remained subdued and mainly directionless on Friday," said Piotr Czyzewski of ING bank in Warsaw. @

Analysts expect the crown to weaken by as much as 15 percent over the next several months as inflated interest rates are slashed and said that the Czech unit may lose some ground next week amid uncertainty surrounding the vote of confidence.
Some two weeks ago the crown's tumble pulled the zloty down over two percent against the currency basket to just above parity, before the Polish unit recovered some lost ground.
Dealers said it was still not clear how the zloty would be effected next week by foreign inflows into Bank Handlowy's one billion zloty public offer. @
Some said the vast majority of inflows would probably go through the post-trade fixing with the central bank, while others said these would give the zloty some support next week.
On Friday, the zloty was fixed at 3.2370 to the dollar and at 1.8640 to the mark. It was at 1.48 percent from parity, unchanged from last week's close.
Analysts said that despite earlier signals of renewed foreign interest in Polish treasuries, investors were cautious when rebuilding positions, especially in shorter-term paper.
At Monday's 1.1 billion zloty T-bill auction yields are expected to hold flat with limited demand from abroad. @
"Foreigners may show up at Monday's tender, but it seems that they are more interested in bonds at the moment," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Dealers said some foreign investors sold T-bills in secondary trade this week to secure funds for the estimated $60 million of fixed bonds they bought last Wednesday, without going through the foreign exchange market.
At Monday's tender the average yield of the 39-week bill, offered for the first time in 1997, should be between the 52-week yield of 21.45 percent and the 26-week yield of 21.37. @
The only other paper on offer on Monday, the 13-week bill, should fall slightly from 20.87 percent, under pressure from domestic corporate bids.
"The shorter-term bills should yield around 20.80-20.85 percent and the 39-week bills around 21.40 percent," said Wojciech Labryga, dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
Dealers said future yield movements were difficult to forecast because the ministry had not yet published its monthly T-bill offer schedule for the month of June. @
"In the past the ministry has published its schedule in the first days of the month and this month's delay is making any longer-term planning impossible," one dealer in Warsaw said.
